bedlam

BED-luhm -- from 'Bethlehem,' the name of a former London hospital for the mentally ill. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Bedlam is a scene of wild uproar and confusion.

The backstage hallway was pure bedlam ten minutes before the show, with costumes, cues, and last-minute rewrites flying everywhere.

Example

The instant the power went out during the championship game, every phone flashlight came on, people started shouting directions in the dark, and someone knocked over an entire table of concession snacks.

That sudden, noisy, out-of-control chaos -- with everyone shouting and nothing under control -- is exactly what bedlam describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

uproar: An uproar is a burst of loud, noisy reaction to one specific thing -- a crowd shouting over a referee's call -- and it can happen in an otherwise orderly room. Bedlam is bigger than noise alone: the whole scene has tipped into confusion, with people moving and shouting in every direction at once.

mayhem: Mayhem is disorder with a violent, destructive edge -- things get knocked over, broken, or hurt. Bedlam stresses the swirl of noise and confused people rather than damage; a room in bedlam is deafening and out of control, but nothing has to be destroyed.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

tranquility: a state of calm and peacefulness

orderliness: a well-organized, systematic state

Where it sits · how loud and crowded the disorder is — chaos → bedlam → pandemonium

chaos vs. bedlam: Chaos is simply a lack of order, and it can be completely silent -- a chaotic desk buried in papers makes no sound at all. Bedlam is louder and more crowded: it adds a mass of people, shouting and moving in every direction.

pandemonium vs. bedlam: Pandemonium pushes past even bedlam -- bedlam is a scene already out of control, while pandemonium is its louder, deafening peak, the split second an entire crowd erupts at once.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — Bedlam

root — Bedlam: a folk-corruption of 'Bethlehem,' after London's St. Mary of Bethlehem psychiatric hospital (Middle English)

Put it together

Put it together: Bedlam began as a nickname for London's Bethlehem hospital, notorious for the noise and disorder inside it -- over time the word drifted from that one building to describe any scene of wild uproar and confusion.

Use the root in a new word: Bethlehem

Use the root in a new word: Bethlehem: Say 'Bethlehem' quickly and carelessly for a few hundred years and it wears down to 'bedlam' -- the chaos word is simply the name of London's Hospital of St Mary of Bethlehem, ground smooth by everyday speech. The place name is still hiding inside the word: Beth-le-hem, bed-l-am.

Word Choice

Bedlam almost always describes a scene involving people -- a crowded, noisy place suddenly out of control -- rather than a quiet mess like a messy desk.
